lessons.title: Lesson 1: Writing a project charter with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page charter that defines the project's goal, scope and success.
This lesson builds toward: Given the key facts of a real or practice project, you will write a one-page charter that states the goal, scope, sponsor, budget, deadline and success measures, with every AI mistake corrected and the sponsor's agreement noted.
A project charter is the project's birth certificate. It says why the project exists, what it will deliver, what is in and out of scope, who the sponsor is, the rough budget and deadline, and how you will know it succeeded. It is like a mission order: purpose, end state, constraints.
Give AI the facts and let it draft: "Write a one-page project charter. Project: veterans' job fair at the community center on March 15. Goal: 30 employers, 200 attendees. Budget: $3,000. Sponsor: the center's director. Out of scope: catering beyond coffee."
Then fix it. AI may invent numbers, stakeholders or goals. Every fact must be yours. Get the sponsor to agree to the charter before work starts; it stops arguments later about what the project was supposed to do.
Step by step:
- Write the purpose, goal, deadline, budget and sponsor.
- List what is in scope and out of scope.
- Ask AI to draft a one-page charter.
- Correct anything AI invented.
- Get the sponsor's agreement.
Words to know:
- Project charter: a short document that authorizes a project and states its goal, scope and limits.
- Scope: the work the project will and will not do.
- Sponsor: the person who supports and approves the project.
- Stakeholder: anyone affected by or involved in the project.
Try it now: Choose a real or practice project. Write its key facts, have AI draft a one-page charter, and mark everything you corrected.
You can now write a one-page project charter with AI help.

check.q: What does scope mean in a project charter?
options: What the project will and will not do
check.why: Scope sets the edges of the project: what is in and what is out.

check.q: AI's draft charter lists a budget you never gave it. What would you do?
options: Keep it because it sounds right
Delete the budget line from every document
Replace it with the real budget from the sponsor and mark the correction
Ask the team to vote on a budget
check.why: AI fills gaps with guesses; the real budget comes from the sponsor.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Breaking the work down and scheduling it
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Turn the charter into a work breakdown structure and a schedule with milestones.
This lesson builds toward: Starting from your charter, you will create a work breakdown structure and a schedule with durations, dependencies and milestones, with at least four milestones and AI time estimates checked.
A work breakdown structure (WBS) breaks the whole project into smaller pieces until each piece is a task one person can do in a few days. For a job fair: venue, employers, marketing, volunteers, day-of logistics, follow-up, each split into tasks.
Ask AI: "From this charter, create a WBS with phases and tasks. Then estimate a duration for each task and list which tasks depend on others." Dependencies matter: you cannot print flyers until the venue and date are confirmed.
Turn it into a schedule in a spreadsheet or free tool, working back from the deadline. Mark milestones, the big checkpoints like "venue booked" or "20 employers confirmed". Check AI's time estimates against your own experience; it tends to be too optimistic.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for a WBS with phases and tasks.
- Split any task bigger than a few days.
- Add durations and dependencies.
- Build a schedule backward from the deadline.
- Mark at least four milestones.
Words to know:
- WBS: work breakdown structure: the whole project broken into smaller tasks.
- Dependency: a task that cannot start until another finishes.
- Milestone: a key checkpoint in a project.
Try it now: Use AI to create a WBS for your project, then build a simple schedule in a spreadsheet with durations, dependencies and at least four milestones.
You can now break a project into tasks and schedule them with milestones.

options: A key point that shows a major part is done
The longest task in the schedule
check.why: A milestone marks a key result, such as "venue booked".

check.q: Your WBS has a task called "Plan the event" that will take six weeks. What would you do?
options: Break it into smaller tasks one person can do in a few days
check.why: WBS tasks should be small enough for one person in a few days.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Assigning roles with a RACI chart
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a RACI chart so everyone knows who does, decides and is informed.
This lesson builds toward: Given the project's main tasks, you will build a RACI chart that shows who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed, with exactly one Accountable person per task and balanced work.
Confusion about who does what sinks projects. A RACI chart lists tasks down the side and people across the top, and marks each box: R for Responsible (does the work), A for Accountable (owns the result and signs off; only one per task), C for Consulted (gives input) and I for Informed (kept updated).
Ask AI: "Make a RACI chart for these tasks and roles: [tasks], [people or roles]." Then check: does every task have exactly one A? Is anyone overloaded with R's? Is anyone Consulted on everything, slowing things down?
Share the RACI with the team and sponsor. When questions come up, like who approves the flyer, point to the chart.
Step by step:
- List the main tasks and the people or roles.
- Ask AI to draft a RACI chart.
- Check each task has exactly one A.
- Balance the R's so nobody is overloaded.
- Share it with the team and sponsor.
Words to know:
- RACI chart: a table showing who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each task.
- Accountable: the one person who owns the result and signs off.
Try it now: Have AI draft a RACI chart for your project's main tasks. Fix it so every task has exactly one A and the work is balanced.
You can now build and check a RACI chart that makes roles clear.

check.q: In a RACI chart, what does "C" mean?
options: Consulted: asked for input before decisions
check.why: Consulted people give input before the work or decision.

check.q: Two people are marked Accountable for the same task. What would you do?
options: Choose one person to be Accountable
Keep both so the work gets done
check.why: Each task needs exactly one Accountable person who owns the result.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Keeping a risk register
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify, rate and plan responses for project risks with AI help.
This lesson builds toward: Given AI's brainstorm of project risks, you will rate the five most real risks and choose a response and owner for each, using avoid, reduce, transfer or accept correctly.
A risk is something that might happen and would affect the project. A risk register lists each risk, how likely it is, how bad the impact would be, the response plan and an owner who watches it.
Ask AI: "List ten risks for this project [paste charter], rate likelihood and impact as low, medium or high, and suggest a response for each." Responses: avoid it, reduce it, transfer it (for example, insurance or a contract) or accept it with a backup plan.
Keep only the risks that are real for your project, add any AI missed, and review the register every week. Military planners call this thinking through branches and sequels; civilians call it risk management.
Step by step:
- Ask AI to brainstorm risks from your charter.
- Rate likelihood and impact.
- Choose a response: avoid, reduce, transfer or accept.
- Give each risk an owner.
- Review the register weekly.
Words to know:
- Risk: something that might happen and affect the project.
- Risk register: a list of risks with ratings, responses and owners.
- Mitigation: steps to reduce a risk's chance or impact.
Try it now: Have AI brainstorm risks for your project. Keep the five most real, rate them, choose responses and assign owners.
You can now build and maintain a risk register with AI help.

check.q: Which risk response means making a risk less likely or less harmful?
check.why: Reducing lowers the chance or the damage of a risk.

check.q: AI lists 25 possible risks for your job fair. What would you do?
options: Pick the one AI lists first
Keep the five most real, rate them and assign owners
check.why: A useful register focuses on the most real risks, each with a response and owner.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Writing status reports that people read
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short weekly status report with a clear red, yellow or green status.
This lesson builds toward: For one week of the project, you will write a half-page status report with an honest red, yellow or green status and decisions needed, with every date and number checked.
A status report keeps the sponsor and team informed. Keep it to half a page: overall status (green on track, yellow at risk, red off track), what got done this week, what is next, risks and issues, and decisions needed from the sponsor.
Paste your schedule updates and notes into AI and ask: "Write a half-page weekly status report with overall status color, accomplishments, next steps, risks and issues, and decisions needed. Be direct."
Be honest about yellow and red. Bad news early is a gift: it gives the sponsor time to help. Hiding problems until the deadline is the fastest way to lose trust. Check every date and number AI wrote.
Step by step:
- Update the schedule and risk register.
- Paste notes and updates into AI.
- Ask for a half-page report with a status color.
- Check every date and number.
- Send it on the same day each week.
Words to know:
- Status report: a regular update on a project's progress, risks and needs.
- Issue: a problem that is happening now, unlike a risk that might happen.
- RAG status: red, amber (yellow) or green: a quick signal of project health.
Try it now: Write a weekly status report for your project (real or imagined week 3) with AI help. Include an honest status color and at least one decision needed.
You can now write a clear, honest weekly status report with AI help.

check.q: What does a yellow status usually mean?
options: There is a problem that may affect the plan if not fixed
check.why: Yellow is a warning: at risk but still recoverable.

check.q: You need the sponsor to approve extra money this week. What would you do in the status report?
options: Leave it out to keep the report green
Mention it only in person next month
List it clearly under decisions needed
check.why: Decisions needed should be easy to see so the sponsor can act.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Closing the project and capturing lessons learned
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Close a project properly and run a lessons-learned review.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of a project, you will run a blame-free lessons-learned review and close the project against the charter, answering all four review questions and storing the files.
Many projects just fade out. A proper close confirms the goals were met (compare to the charter), hands over anything that continues, pays final bills, thanks the team and stores the files where others can find them.
A lessons-learned review, like an after-action review, asks: what did we plan, what happened, why, and what should we do differently next time? Collect input from everyone, including what went well.
AI can sort the input: "Group these lessons-learned comments into themes and write three recommendations for future projects." Keep it blame-free, focus on the process, and check that the summary is fair. If you want to grow in project management, the Project Management Institute offers credentials such as CAPM, PMP and an AI-focused PMI-CPMAI; check pmi.org for current requirements and fees.
Step by step:
- Compare results to the charter's goals.
- Hand over ongoing work and pay final bills.
- Run a blame-free lessons-learned review.
- Use AI to group comments and draft recommendations.
- Store all files and thank the team.
Words to know:
- Closeout: the formal end of a project.
- Lessons learned: what a team learned that should change how future projects are run.
- After-action review: a structured look back: planned, happened, why, what to change.
Official sources:
- Project Management Institute: certifications
Try it now: Final task: finish your project plan with charter, WBS, schedule with milestones, RACI, risk register and one status report, then write a lessons-learned template with the four review questions. Mark every place you corrected AI.
You can now plan, run and close a project using AI to draft documents while you make the decisions.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Charter Missing the goal, scope, sponsor, deadline or success measures, or AI guesses left in. One page with all parts, and every AI correction marked. Also lists what is out of scope and how success will be measured. WBS and schedule Tasks are too big, or fewer than four milestones. Small tasks, dependencies and at least four milestones, with AI estimates checked. Schedule built backward from the deadline with some buffer time. RACI chart A task has no Accountable person or more than one. Exactly one A per task and work spread fairly. Notes who must be consulted before key decisions. Risk register Fewer than five risks, or no responses or owners. Five real risks rated, each with a response and an owner. Shows when each risk will be reviewed and what would trigger action. Status report Status color is not honest, or dates and numbers are unchecked. Half a page with an honest color, progress, next steps and decisions needed. A busy sponsor could act on it in under a minute. Closeout and lessons learned No lessons-learned template, or it blames people. A blame-free template with the four review questions. Also plans how results will be compared to the charter and where files will be stored. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is the purpose of a lessons-learned review?
options: To improve the process for the next project
To end the project without paperwork
check.why: Lessons learned are blame-free and focus on what to change next time.

check.q: The project is done. What would you do before calling it closed?
options: Start the next project right away
Compare results to the charter and store the files
check.why: Closeout checks results against the charter and saves the records.
